opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what struck me most was how *simple* the core idea was, and how well it worked anyway.

When I got to OpenAI, I'd been working mostly on language grounding and reinforcement learning, where you spend a lot of effort designing task-specific architectures. The bet with GPT was almost the opposite: take one fairly generic model, train it on a large amount of unlabeled text with just next-word prediction, and see whether that gives you representations useful for many tasks. Then you fine-tune lightly on whatever downstream task you care about.

At the time that wasn't obvious. People were using pretrained word embeddings, and there was work on pretrained LSTMs, but the default was still that each task needed its own carefully engineered model. So when we saw a single pretrained transformer, with minimal task-specific changes, improving results across a broad range of benchmarks like entailment, question answering, and classification, that was the surprising part. It suggested the pretraining objective was capturing something general about language, not just surface statistics.

The transformer mattered a lot here. Compared to recurrent models, it handled longer context more gracefully and scaled more cleanly with compute, and you could see that the model was using that longer context. That made us think the gains weren't a fluke of one setup; there was a real trend.

The other thing, looking back, is that we weren't thinking of it primarily as a *generative* system in the way people use these models today. "Generative" was in the name, but the main framing was pretraining as a route to better understanding and transfer. We noticed signs of zero-shot behavior, where the model could do a bit of a task without fine-tuning, but it was more of a curiosity in the paper. The idea that you could drop fine-tuning and just prompt a much larger model came into focus later. So it was a bit of a seed. We could tell something interesting was there, but I don't think any of us fully anticipated how far scaling that recipe would go.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me most was how simple the recipe was. We weren't doing anything exotic. It was a transformer decoder, trained to predict the next token on a big pile of books, and then fine-tuned on downstream tasks. At the time, the field was full of these very carefully engineered, task-specific architectures. You'd have one model for entailment, another for question answering, each with its own clever attention mechanism or memory module. And here was this one generic thing that just read a lot of text and then did well on almost all of them.

What surprised me was the transfer. We had a hypothesis that language modeling would be a good pretraining objective, because to predict the next word well you have to pick up some syntax, some world knowledge, some reasoning. But I don't think any of us expected the gains to be as consistent as they were across twelve or so benchmarks. That was the moment where I remember thinking, okay, this is not a trick, something real is happening.

The other thing, which is almost funny in hindsight, was how small it was. A little over a hundred million parameters, trained on the BookCorpus, which is maybe seven thousand books. We thought of that as a lot of data. And even at that scale you could already see hints of zero-shot behavior. We had a small section in the paper where we just prompted the model without fine-tuning and it did better than chance on some tasks. We treated it as a curiosity. In retrospect, that was the most important result in the paper, and we buried it in a figure.

So I'd say the takeaway for me was less about the architecture and more about the lesson that a general objective plus scale can beat a lot of hand-crafted structure. I had spent years working on language grounding and reinforcement learning, building fairly specialized systems, and this was a bit of a humbling experience. It changed how I thought about what to work on next.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was how much you could get out of a seemingly simple objective: predicting the next word. To do that well across a lot of different text, the model has to pick up patterns that turn out to be useful for other tasks, too.

The exciting question was whether we could learn those patterns once, through pretraining, and then adapt the same model to different problems. With the original GPT, we still fine-tuned on individual tasks, but the foundation was shared. That felt like a promising shift away from designing a separate architecture for every problem.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was the idea that you could learn useful representations just by predicting the next word, and then adapt the same model to different tasks. Instead of building a separate architecture for each task, you could pretrain a transformer on text and fine-tune it with relatively small changes. That suggested a much more general approach to language learning. The exciting question was how far that simple training objective could take us.
